findings.reason: In this line the source prints ח, not ה. Its left leg is joined at the top, unlike the open ה of שֶׁהוּא in the other five lines. Record it as printed and apply sic/corr later.

The first letter is the Rashi/Vaybertaytsh shin, which looks like a square ס. The real Rashi ס on this page, in סוגרים הארון, has a different shape that looks like ק. The German word is schaltet … ein.
The city name is the same word in the same typeface in both rubrics, and each time the source prints a patah under the alef. The human answer for the second rubric (325) already reads פֿראַנקפֿורט.

The human's ך in 324 was marked tentative. The last letter has a hooked head and a short descender, which is the Rashi final tsadi. A Rashi ך is a straight long stroke, as in כחך (נאָך) in the next rubric. The letter is also different from the ז in עז and מייזטען. Metz = מעץ.
This is the same letter in the same typeface as the city name in the first rubric, and it should match that rubric: Rashi final tsadi.

uncertainties.question: Only needed if the human wants to confirm: is the last letter of the city name a final tsadi (hooked head, short tail) rather than a final kaf (straight long stroke like the end of כחך)? The same glyph appears in both rubrics. I read it as ץ.
